summary: Google's world headquarters sits here, but so does Shoreline Lake — a 50-acre artificial saltwater lake at the edge of the San Francisco Bay where you can windsurf on your lunch break, a juxtaposition that captures Mountain View's strange duality. The city occupies a remarkably flat stretch of the Santa Clara Valley floor, squeezed between the bay's marshy wetlands to the northeast and the foothills of the Santa Cruz Mountains to the southwest, which means winter sunsets drop behind visible ridgelines while morning light rolls in unobstructed. Castro Street, the compact downtown spine, delivers a genuine walkable strip of sit-down restaurants, independent coffee shops, and a well-attended farmers' market — but step a few blocks in any direction and the texture shifts abruptly to low-slung office parks and quiet residential blocks bisected by the Central Expressway and Highway 101, fragmenting the city into distinct zones that don't always connect gracefully on foot. The affordability math is stark: a median home price north of $1.9 million against a median household income around $180,000 produces a price-to-income ratio above 10:1, and even median rent at nearly $3,000 claims a significant share of that income. With 290-plus sunny days and average highs hovering around 70°F year-round, the climate barely registers as a variable — which may be why the real dividing line in Mountain View isn't weather or even commute, but whether you work for one of the massive campuses lining Shoreline Boulevard or commute past them on your way somewhere else.
